candidates.label: Lycaonia (label point)
candidates.support: Lycaonia's identity as the region containing Lystra and Derbe is undisputed. The label point is Wikidata's point for the region, in the Lycaonian plain north of Lystra and Derbe and about 47 km from Iconium's pin. Pleiades' 'Lykaonia', after the Barrington Atlas, has only an approximate point about 70 km to the southwest, near Lystra's pin.

summary.text: Lycaonia was a plain in the central-southern part of Asia Minor. Acts records that after Paul and Barnabas were driven out of Iconium, they 'fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region,' where the residents spoke 'the language of Lycaonia.' On this map, Lycaonia means the western, Roman part of the region, where Lystra and Derbe lay.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that in Paul's time Lycaonia had two parts. The western part was one of the 'regions' into which the Roman province of Galatia was divided. The eastern part, known as Lycaonia Antiochiana, had been placed under the client king Antiochus of Commagene in AD 37. Acts 14:6, which names only Lystra and Derbe, describes the western, Roman part, and this map follows that sense; the eastern part lay outside the province at this project's about AD 50 date.

scripture.textWEB: they became aware of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region.
When the multitude saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!”

politicalHistory.note: Includes Pisidia, Lycaonia (the western part) and Paphlagonia, which had already joined the province of Galatia (Pisidia and Lycaonia in 25 BC on King Amyntas's death; Paphlagonia in 6 BC) before this note's window begins. Vespasian detached most of Pisidia to the new province of Lycia and Pamphylia in AD 74; no source describing exactly where that internal line ran was found, so this area is kept whole rather than guessing at a split.
